reps.md:
Plovdiv is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and it looks it. Three granite hills rise out of a flat plain beside the Maritsa river, and people have lived on them for thousands of years. The Romans knew the city as Philippopolis, after Philip II of Macedon, and the Roman stadium still runs under the main street.

## Layers

**Roman and Ottoman.** You can see Roman mosaics in a road underpass, a Roman aqueduct in the middle of a road, and the Ottoman hamams (the Chifte, shut; the Orta Mezar, a burnt shell). The clock tower on Sahat Tepe dates from the 17th century in its first, wooden form.

**The Revival and the Unification.** In the 19th century the city's merchants built the painted houses of the Old Town. Plovdiv was the capital of Eastern Rumelia, and on 6 September 1885 it was the scene of the Unification with the rest of Bulgaria.

**The tobacco city.** Plovdiv was a tobacco town. The brick warehouses of Tobacco Town are the physical record, and the 1953 workers' revolt is its dark footnote.

**Socialist Plovdiv.** From 1944 the regime rebuilt the city in concrete: the Party House, the House of Science, the Trakiya estate, the Brotherly Mound, the ritual houses and mosaics. That layer is what this map is for.

## How to use the map
Start with the Concrete centre walk, add the Old Town walks for the layers, and take Karshiyaka and Trakiya if you want to see the city most people live in. Many of the best things are small or locked, so the guide texts say what you can actually see.

Plovdiv has one of the best collections of socialist-era architecture and art in Bulgaria, and unlike Sofia's it sits right next to a living old town.

**Start with the Brotherly Mound.** Bratska Mogila (1974) is a ring of concrete slabs echoing a Thracian burial mound, with a hall of urns inside. The hall is locked, but the exterior is the point.

**The centre.** Kino Kosmos (1960–64, under reconstruction), the Youth House, the House of Science (1985) and the Party House (1969) cover thirty years of the regime's architecture within a few hundred metres.

**The rites.** The regime built houses for its own ceremonies: the Lotus Hall for naming newborns, the House of the Newlyweds, the Mother and Child House and the House of the Deceased. Two have since become kitsch exhibits.

**Estates and art.** Trakiya (252 blocks) and the Big Giant megablock show where people lived. Mosaics by Kmetova and Leviev, and the Gagarin wall, show the art that went with it.

**The dump.** Behind a fence in Karshiyaka lie the statues the city took down in the 1990s.

Start with: Bratska Mogila, then Tobacco Town and the concrete centre walk.

Plovdiv's small memorials tell a harder story than its monuments.

**1876 and 1878.** The priest Nikola Belchov was hanged in July 1876 after the April Uprising; a plaque by Viktor Todorov marks the place near the Roman stadium. The bronze head was stolen and returned.

**1943.** In the yard of the former Jewish school the Metropolitan Kiril stopped the deportation of the city's Jews. A plaque and the 1998 Monument of Gratitude mark it, next to the Zion synagogue.

**The communist era.** The 1953 tobacco-workers' revolt has no plaque. The political prisoners' memorial on the old gallows site is a decaying remnant. The jazz violinist Sasho Sladura, who died in a labour camp in 1961, has a statue you can sit on. Father Kamen Vichev, shot in 1952, has another.

**After 1989.** The statues of the regime were dumped in a yard in Sheker mahala. A 1997 protest heap of stones sits in the Dondukov garden, and may soon be removed.

Start with: the Jewish school and synagogue, then Belchov and Sladura.

The thinkers' layer in Plovdiv is thin but real, and several places are still open.

**Alafrangite** is an 18th-century house and 1960s bohemian haunt, and it is open: the one place on this map where you can sit in a thinkers' tavern that still works.

**Kristal**, the 1960s writers' café (Gencho Stoev, Konstantin Pavlov, the Drama Theatre actors), is now the Download rock bar and leaves its address on 31 December 2026.

**Slaveykov's café** on Vazrazhdane Square is closed for restoration with no date. Vazov's gazebo is in a private yard.

**Others:** Zlatna Krusha (1929, bohemians), the site of the First Shumen Beerhouse (1913, the intelligentsia after premieres), and the Lavrenov statue on a bench.

Start with: Alafrangite, then Kristal before the end of the year.

**Walking tour.** Free Plovdiv Tour runs a socialist-architecture walk on Saturdays at 11:00 from the municipality building. Check that it is still running.

**Tickets.** The Irini underpass building costs about €2–3.50 and is open daily 09:00–18:00. The clock tower is open about 08:00–18:00. The Hippocrates pharmacy museum is open Tuesday–Sunday. The Regional History Museum is open Monday–Saturday. Check prices before you go.

**Closed or changing.** Chifte Hamam is closed (exterior only). Kino Kosmos reopens in 2027. Kafene Starinnoto is closed for restoration. Rock Bar Download leaves Lady Strangford 5 on 31 December 2026. The Bunardzhik shelter opens only for events. The Dondukov garden's protest heap may be removed.

**Day trips.** Buzludzha: about two hours by bus via Kazanlak, then a taxi; private tours from about €270 per vehicle; the interior is sealed. Perushtitsa needs a car or taxi. The Aviation Museum at Krumovo is open Wednesday–Sunday 09:00–18:00.
